awd_titl_txt: I-Corps: Translation Potential of Diagnostic Markers for Gastrointestinal Disease
awd_abstract_narration:
This I-Corps project focuses on the development of a point-of-care diagnostic test for a common digestive system disease, irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). IBS symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, constipation and diarrhea. IBS is associated with psychological disorders such as anxiety and stress and affects 25-45 million people in the U.S. and 10-15% people worldwide. IBS significantly affects the quality of life of patients, resulting in days off work or missed school, and costs healthcare systems more than $30 billion/year. Doctors cannot diagnose IBS based on symptoms alone, as people who do not have this disease may also show similar symptoms, such as diarrhea and constipation, due to other causes. Currently IBS is diagnosed by the process of elimination, where patients often go through several tests to rule out other issues, and even then, there is a chance of misdiagnosis. This project aims to address this issue by offering a point-of-care diagnostic test using patient biomarkers for early diagnosis of this disease. 

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of a point-of-care diagnostic test that can be used by gastroenterologists and physicians in clinical settings to diagnose irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). This solution is based on the detection of specific metabolites that are present only in the human patient samples with IBS using a paper-based assay. The test works by using special proteins that recognize and bind to certain target molecules (metabolites) in a sample. When this binding happens, the target molecules push out indicator compounds that were originally attached to the proteins. This change creates a color signal, which reveals which metabolites are present and in what amount. The resulting indicators are chromatographically separated using a paper device, allowing the results to be seen and interpreted visually. The test is expected to lead to definitive and rapid diagnosis of IBS, allowing timely and targeted approaches to managing the disease and improving patient care and well-being.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This project focuses on the development of a point-of-care diagnostic test for a common digestive system disease. Its symptoms include abdominal pain, bloating, constipation and diarrhea. It is also associated with psychological disorders such as anxiety and stress. It affects 25-45 million people in the US and 10-15% of the world population. It significantly affects the quality of life of patients resulting in days off work or missing school. Healthcare costs of this disease result in more than $30 billion/year. It is not fully understood how this disease develops. It is not caused by tumors or biochemical abnormalities. Doctors cannot diagnose it based on symptoms alone as people who do not have this disease may also show similar symptoms such as diarrhea, constipation etc. There are no diagnostic tests available specifically for this disease and routine medical tests such as, X-rays, blood tests and endoscopic exams, show normal results. Currently it is diagnosed by the process of elimination. Patients often have to go through a number of tests to rule out other issues before this disease diagnosis is determined and even then, there is a chance of misdiagnosis. There is thus a strong need for a specific diagnostic test for this disease. We are developing a diagnostic test using markers discovered by us. Early diagnosis of this disease will help avoid symptoms flare ups, reduce psychological comorbidities, improve quality of life and reduce national health care burden.

This I-Corps project utilizes experiential learning coupled with a first-hand investigation of the industry ecosystem to assess the translation potential of the technology. This solution is based on the development of a diagnostic test. Specific metabolites that are present only in the human patient samples compared to healthy controls are identified and validated. Paper-based assays to chemically detect these metabolites in patient samples that will offer rapid, low-cost, point-of-care diagnostics are being developed. The test is based on the binding of these specific metabolites by certain standard proteins resulting in displacement of indicator molecules from protein association and the ultimate colorimetric readout of the liberated indicators. Liberation of indicator molecules is dependent on the presence and identity of human sample metabolites. The resulting indicators are chromatographically separated on the paper device and visualized. The test is expected to lead to definitive and rapid diagnosis of this gastrointestinal disorder allowing timely and specific approaches to manage the disease. 

As part of the NSF I-Corps program, we went to several conferences and also interviewed a number of people through other avenues. We interviewed several gastroenterologists, GI health care people (e.g. GI Fellows and GI PAs), primary care physicians, Big Pharma leaders (CEOs, managing directors, project managers, and founders of companies), pharm sales representatives, and patients. Through the customer discovery, we made major pivots as we learned that ‘unmet need’ is our value proposition. We also learned the important aspects of customer segments for our product, for example, patients are not decision makers in their disease management, primary care physicians do not take care of specialized GI diseases and pharmaceutical agents can be allies, but not customer segment. Thus another major pivot we made was that gastroenterologists are our ‘customer segment’. We also identified biotech companies specializing in paper-based diagnostics as our channel partners and existing pharma focused on gastroenterology products as our distribution partners. We then included these two cohorts in our interviews. We were able to identify a suitable channel partner, with whom we are currently collaborating to develop our diagnostic test. Through the NSF I-Corps, we also learned about modes of customer relationships for our product, for example, conference-based awareness through GI conferences, clinic educational materials, booklets, test guides, targeted patient marketing through TV spots and social media, doctor-pharma collaborations through joint webinars and case talks and post-sales support through check ins and feedback portal. We also identified clinical laboratory services, pharmacy and point-of-care (hospitals, physician offices) as channels. We defined our key activities as production of paper-based tests, sample analysis and clinical validation and intellectual property and regulatory strategy management. We also identified our revenue stream to be direct diagnostic sales and licensing fees. Other aspects of business canvas model such as key resources and cost structure also were enriched through our learning during the cohort. We started this journey thinking that we are going to make a home diagnostic test. We made a major pivot through our learnings and decided that our test is going to be a clinical test. The customer feedback during NSF National I-Corps Program also directed us to carry out the proposed work to demonstrate minimal viable product (MVP) capability of our diagnostic.
